thread.title: How an Upstart Smartphone Maker Is Trying to Compete with Apple and Samsung

title: How an Upstart Smartphone Maker Is Trying to Compete with Apple and Samsung
text:
How an Upstart Smartphone Maker Is Trying to Compete with Apple and Samsung Essential is playing David to the smartphone industry's Goliaths. May2,20186:49PMEDT The Essential smartphone, with an optional 360-degree camera.
Competing with titans is never easy. But Essential's smartphone, designed by Android creator Andy Rubin, is making a go of challenging the dominant smartphone makers, Apple Inc. ( AAPL ) and Samsung ( SSNLF ) , which each ship hundreds of millions of devices a year.
By contrast, Essential has yet to ship even a million units of its high-end phone, said Niccolo de Masi, Essential's president, speaking at the Collision tech conference in New Orleans on Wednesday. But de Masi said his company intends to compete with the giants by offering a comparably-featured phone at a much better price -- its phone costs about $500, half the cost of the iPhone X and about two-thirds the cost of the Samsung Galaxy S9 -- and by being innovative in its features and design.
In fact, de Masi said he likens Essential in some ways to Tesla ( TSLA ) , which he pointed out is on pace to make about 100,000 Model 3's a year, just 1% of the number of vehicles that a company like GM makes annually.
"I think that kind of success and innovation is what we will showcase in the coming product cycle," de Masi said. Essential's president Niccolo de Masi
Essential started in 2015 and begin shipping its first phones last fall. They boast a titanium case, the largest screen-to-body ratio in the business and a unique magnetic connector that allows you to snap on different accessories, such as a 360 degree camera, as well as charge the phone and transfer data. The initial reviews were critical of the phone camera's software, but de Masi said the company's worked hard to update and improve those features quickly.
The future plan is to compete with proprietary AI-powered software that allows users to more easily interact with their phones and with other devices, de Masi said.
"We're believers that in the future -- the internet of things and a multi-device world -- AI has to play a presentation layer for consumers," de Masi said. "We won't be able to get to the future if you have to interact with dozens and dozens of apps that have to be updated, and that you have to log into."
Essential doesn't have a launch date yet for this new software, but de Masi said that consumers should start see something within the next year. Meanwhile, it remains to be seen to what extent Apple can improve its own AI-based phone interface, Siri, which by many people's reckoning has fallen behind the voice assistants developed by Amazon ( AMZN ) and Alphabet's ( GOOGL ) Google.
"It's a long-term game, no doubt about it," de Masi said.
